5	
6	# Skill Author
7	
8	Helps you write **new agent skills** that follow the best-practices documented at
9	https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/ — without you having to re-read those pages
10	every time. Pairs with `skill-creator` (which handles eval/iterate/optimize loops
11	once a draft exists).
12	
13	## When to use this vs `skill-creator`
14	
15	| Task | Use |
16	|---|---|
17	| "I want to make a new skill for X" | **skill-author** (scaffold + author) |
18	| "Scaffold the SKILL.md / a reference / a script" | **skill-author** |
19	| "Lint this skill draft" | **skill-author** |
20	| "My skill isn't triggering when I want it to" | `skill-creator` (description optimization) |
21	| "Run test cases against my skill, benchmark it" | `skill-creator` (eval loop) |
22	| "Compare two versions of my skill" | `skill-creator` (blind comparison) |
23	
24	If both apply, start here, then hand off to `skill-creator` once the draft is solid.
25	
26	## Workflow
27	
28	### 1. Capture intent (1 minute)
29	
30	Before scaffolding, get four answers — usually just by asking the user:
31	
32	1. **What does it do?** (one sentence)
33	2. **When should it trigger?** (specific user phrases / contexts)
34	3. **What does it output?** (file, command result, plan, prose)
35	4. **Is the output objectively verifiable?** (decides whether `skill-creator` evals are worth the effort later)
36	
37	Write these four down before touching files. They become the seeds for the
38	description, the workflow body, and the future eval set.
39	
40	### 2. Scaffold
41	
42	Use `scripts/new-skill.sh` to produce the directory layout. The script
43	auto-detects **scope** (where to put the skill) and fans out discovery
44	symlinks for non-universal agents so the skill is loadable immediately.
45	
46	```bash
47	bash skills/local/skill-author/scripts/new-skill.sh <skill-name>
48	```
49	
50	Three scopes (auto-detected; override with `--local` / `--project` / `--global`):
51	
52	| Scope | Canonical dir | Symlinks created |
53	|---|---|---|
54	| **LOCAL** (this publishing repo: vendor.yaml / skills/local/ found walking up) | `<repo>/skills/local/<name>/` (or `skills/vendor/<name>/` with `--vendor`) | `.agents/skills/<name>` + `.claude/skills/<name>` -> `../../skills/{local,vendor}/<name>` |
55	| **PROJECT** (inside another git repo) | `<repo>/.agents/skills/<name>/` (universal agents — Cursor / Codex / OpenCode / Warp — pick this up directly) | `.claude/skills/<name>` -> `../../.agents/skills/<name>` (+ any already-present non-universal agent dir at the repo root) |

58	The template's frontmatter has placeholders that lint will reject — this is on

62	> but haven't said whether the skill should live with the project or be

73

77	- **Description must be "pushy"** and include concrete trigger contexts. Naive
78	  descriptions cause undertriggering — the #1 failure mode of new skills. Keep
79	  this within the cross-agent budget: 120-500 chars is the preferred range,
80	  501-900 is valid but context-heavy, 901-1024 is valid but close to hard
81	  loader limits, and >1024 is invalid for Codex/Cursor/spec-aligned skills.
82	- **Gotchas section** — environment-specific facts that defy reasonable
83	  assumptions. The single highest-value section in most skills.
84	- **Output templates** — agents pattern-match against concrete structures more
85	  reliably than they follow prose descriptions of formats.
86	- **Calibrated specificity** — be prescriptive only where the task is fragile;
87	  give the agent freedom (and explain *why*) where multiple approaches are valid.
88	- **Defaults, not menus** — pick one tool/approach and mention alternatives as
89	  escape hatches.

96

98	design is meaningfully different from "regular" CLI script design because the
99	caller is an LLM reading your stderr to decide what to do next. The non-obvious
100	requirements:
101	
102	- No interactive prompts, ever (agents run in non-interactive shells)
103	- `--help` is the primary interface documentation — keep it concise but complete
104	- Errors must say *what was expected* and *what to try*, not just *what failed*
105	- Structured stdout (JSON/CSV/TSV), prose diagnostics to stderr — separate them
106	- `--dry-run` for any destructive operation
107	- Pin versions for `uvx` / `npx` / `pipx` invocations
108	
109	For Python helpers, prefer **PEP 723 inline dependencies** + `uv run` over
110	`requirements.txt` — the script becomes self-contained and the agent doesn't
111	have to set up an environment first.

114	
115	Run the linter before committing or handing off to `skill-creator`:

119	```

124	   hyphen-case and <=64 chars; description has a "use when" trigger phrase,

126	2. **Script hygiene** — every `scripts/*.sh` has a shebang, is executable, and
127	   responds to `--help` (presence of the flag handler, not necessarily a working
128	   script).
129	3. **Reference reachability** — every file in `references/` is mentioned at
130	   least once from `SKILL.md` (no dead reference docs).

193	## Gotchas
194	
195	- **AGENTS.md is a symlink to CLAUDE.md** — edit either one; never replace the
196	  symlink with a real file.
197	- **Skill discovery is one level deep first, then recursive up to 5 levels.**
198	  `skills/local/<name>/SKILL.md` works because of the recursive fallback. Don't
199	  nest skills more than 5 deep or they become invisible.
200	- **`bash 3.2` compatibility** is required for any script that might run on
201	  stock macOS. No `mapfile`, no `${var,,}` lowercasing, no `[[ -v var ]]`.
202	  See `references/script-design.md` for the safe subset.
203	- **`description` is always-on context and has agent-specific hard limits.**
204	  Put concrete trigger phrases in frontmatter, but keep local skills in the

206	  Codex and Cursor/spec-aligned validators can skip the skill entirely.
207	- **Quote any `description` containing `:`, `#`, or leading punctuation.** An
208	  unquoted YAML plain scalar cannot contain `": "` — `npx skills` fails with
209	  "Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings" and drops the skill

 `/Users/david/Documents/Program/agent-skills/skills/local/pueue-job-queue/SKILL.md`

```text
1	---
2	name: pueue-job-queue
3	description: Drive Nukesor/pueue (https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue) for queued, parallel, scheduled, and lightly-DAG'd shell jobs — wraps `pueue add --after`, `pueue status --json`, `pueue log --json`, group-level parallelism, and `pueued` daemon health. Use when the user wants to background long-running shell commands across reboots, queue dozens of jobs with capped parallelism, run a fan-out / fan-in pipeline of shell steps, says "pueue", "pueued", "pueue add", "pueue queue", "pueue group", "task queue for shell", "background this job", or asks how to schedule/parallelize CLI work without a real orchestrator (Airflow/Prefect/Dagster). Good fit for ML sweeps, long-running data pipelines, batched evaluations, scheduled `--delay` jobs, "wait for X then run Y" sequences.
4	---
5	
6	# pueue job queue
7	
8	Pueue is a daemon-backed shell job queue. The daemon (`pueued`) accepts tasks
9	via the `pueue` CLI, runs them across parallelism-capped **groups**, persists
10	state across reboots, and exposes status / logs as JSON. This skill teaches
11	the agent to drive pueue end-to-end: submit single tasks or whole DAGs, cap
12	parallelism per group, block until completion, retrieve logs, and retry.
13	
14	The skill is a **CLI bridge**, not a scheduler. Pueue's `--after` is **AND-only**
15	and **success-only** — that maps cleanly to declarative DAGs and not much
16	beyond. For OR-deps, conditional branching, retry-with-backoff, or distributed
17	scheduling, escalate to a real orchestrator (see "When NOT to use").
18	
19	## When to use
20	
21	- "Run these 30 commands, max 4 at a time" → `pueue group add ml && pueue parallel 4 --group ml` then loop `submit.sh --group ml`.
22	- "Kick off a long training job and let me close my laptop" → `submit.sh -- ./train.sh` (pueue persists across reboots).
23	- "Run task B only after task A finishes successfully" → `submit.sh --after $A_ID -- ./b.sh`.
24	- "Fan out 4 trainings, then evaluate" → `submit-dag.py dag.yaml`.
25	- "Schedule this for tonight" → `submit.sh --delay 6h -- ./nightly.sh`.
26	- "Block until task 17 is done, then tell me what happened" → `wait.py --ids 17`.
27	- The user mentions pueue, pueued, the pueue CLI, or asks about a "task queue for shell jobs".
28	
29	## When NOT to use
30	
31	- **One short shell command** the user wants to run right now. Just run it. Pueue adds daemon overhead for nothing.
32	- **Cross-host *scheduling*** (jobs distributed across N machines) → Airflow / Dagster / Prefect / Slurm. Note this is not the same as driving a *single* remote daemon, which pueue does support — see `references/remote-daemon.md`.
33	- **Conditional / OR / retry-with-backoff dependencies** → real orchestrator. Pueue's `--after` is AND-only and success-only.
34	- **Typed task IO and artifact tracking** (data lineage, cached intermediate outputs) → DVC (`dvc exp run --queue`), Prefect, Airflow.
35	- **Long-running services** (web servers, daemons) → systemd, launchd, supervisord. Pueue is for finite tasks.
36	
37	## Authoritative sources
38	
39	- Repo: https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue
40	- Wiki: https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue/wiki
41	- `pueue --help`, `pueue <subcommand> --help`, `man pueue`
42	
43	## Mental model
44	
45	| Concept | What it is | How to interact |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| **Daemon** (`pueued`) | Long-running process holding queue state. Required. | `pueued -d` to start. `pueue shutdown` to stop. |
48	| **Task** | One shell command, identified by integer id. | `pueue add ...`, `pueue status`, `pueue kill`, `pueue remove`. |
49	| **Group** | Named queue with its own parallelism limit. `default` always exists. | `pueue group add <name>`, `pueue parallel N --group <name>`. |
50	| **Dependency** | Task waits for one or more parents to **succeed** before running. | `pueue add --after <id> --after <id> -- <cmd>`. AND-only, success-only. |
51	| **Status** | Tagged enum: `Queued`, `Running`, `Stashed`, `Paused`, `Locked`, `Done`. `Done` carries a `result` (`Success`, `Killed`, `DependencyFailed`, or `{"Failed": <exit_code>}`). | `pueue status --json`. |
52	
53	## Setup quickstart
54	
55	```bash
56	# 1. Verify daemon is healthy. Auto-start if missing.
57	bash skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/check-daemon.sh --start --json | jq
58	
59	# 2. (Optional) Create a group with 4 parallel slots.
60	pueue group add ml
61	pueue parallel 4 --group ml
62	```
63	
64	For per-OS daemon paths and launchd/systemd setup, read
65	`references/daemon-and-config.md`.
66	
67	## Always pass a label
68	
69	`pueue status` shows the **label** column before the command. In a busy
70	queue, scanning labels is the only way to tell `train.py` runs apart at a
71	glance. **Always pass `--label`** when submitting, and bias toward names
72	that distinguish *this* task from its siblings.
73	
74	Convention:
75	
76	- Shape: `<verb>-<subject>-<key>` (≤30 chars). `verb` = action,
77	  `subject` = artifact, `key` = the variable that distinguishes this run.
78	- Encode the discriminator: seed, dataset slice, model variant, date, host.
79	- Don't restate the command — `train.py --seed 1` becomes label
80	  `train-baseline-seed1`, not `python-train-py-seed-1`.
81	- For DAGs, `submit-dag.py --label-prefix <run>-` makes every task labeled
82	  `<run>-<task_name>` so `wait.py --label-prefix <run>-` selects the whole
83	  graph and `pueue clean` can be filtered later.
84	
85	| Good | Bad |
86	|---|---|
87	| `train-baseline-seed1` | `task1` (no metadata) |
88	| `eval-prod-2026q1` | `python eval.py --quarter 2026q1` (restates cmd) |
89	| `fetch-prices-AAPL` | `fetch-data` (multiple identical labels) |
90	| `nightly-featurize` (DAG) | `step-2-of-5` (rename a step → label rots) |
91	
92	## Workflow A — submit one task
93	
94	```bash
95	bash skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/submit.sh \
96	  --label train-baseline --group ml \
97	  -- python train.py --seed 1
98	# stdout: {"task_id":17,"label":"train-baseline","group":"ml","after":[],...}
99	# stderr: submitted task 17 (group=ml, label=train-baseline)
100	```
101	
102	Capture the id with `jq -r .task_id`. The script wraps `pueue add
103	--print-task-id` and falls back to a status-by-label lookup if the id parse
104	fails (defensive against future format changes).
105	
106	## Workflow B — batched runs with capped parallelism
107	
108	```bash
109	# One-time: create + size the group
110	pueue group add sweep
111	pueue parallel 4 --group sweep
112	
113	# Loop: submit 30 tasks; pueue runs at most 4 at a time
114	for SEED in $(seq 1 30); do
115	  bash skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/submit.sh \
116	    --label "sweep-$SEED" --group sweep \
117	    -- python train.py --seed "$SEED"
118	done
119	
120	# Block until all sweep-* tasks are done
121	skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/wait.py \
122	  --label-prefix sweep- --group sweep
123	```
124	
125	Group parallelism is the parallelism primitive in pueue — there is no
126	per-task pool. Set it once, submit freely.
127	
128	## Workflow C — fan-out / fan-in DAG
129	
130	For multi-task pipelines with success-only dependencies, write a YAML spec
131	and submit it declaratively. **Prefer `--isolated-group`** — it creates a
132	fresh group sized to the DAG's fan-out width and leaves your other groups
133	(especially `default`) untouched:
134	
135	```bash
136	skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/submit-dag.py \
137	  skills/local/pueue-job-queue/assets/dag.example.yaml \
138	  --label-prefix nightly- --isolated-group
139	# stderr: isolated-group: created 'dag-dcda9347' with parallel_tasks=2
140	# stdout: {"tasks":{"fetch":17,...},
141	#          "topo_order":[...],
142	#          "width_per_group":{"dag-dcda9347":2},
143	#          "isolated_group":"dag-dcda9347"}
144	```
145	
146	Each task gets the label `<--label-prefix><task_name>` so you can
147	`wait.py --label-prefix nightly-` later. After the run, clean up with
148	`pueue group remove <name>` (or run `cleanup.sh --remove-empty-groups`).
149	
150	The submitter topo-sorts, validates the graph (cycle detection, unknown
151	references, missing `cmd:`), computes the **DAG width per group** (the
152	minimum `parallel_tasks` needed for fan-out to actually run in parallel),
153	then submits in order — wiring `--after` from the in-flight name→id map.
154	**No partial submits**: validation fails loud before any `pueue add` runs.
155	
156	Three parallelism modes, in order of recommendation:
157	
158	1. **`--isolated-group [NAME]`** (recommended). Fresh group, sized to width,
159	   no side effects on other groups. NAME auto-generates from spec hash if
160	   omitted. Mutually exclusive with `--default-group`.
161	2. **`--auto-parallel`**. Mutates `pueue parallel` on the target group in
162	   place. Use this when the DAG is meant to live in a long-lived shared
163	   group (e.g. `ml`) and that group's parallelism should permanently grow.
164	3. **No flag**. Only warns (in stderr + JSON's `parallelism_warnings`).
165	   Useful in `--dry-run` planning.
166	
167	See `assets/dag.example.yaml` for a 5-task fan-out/fan-in template and
168	`references/dag-patterns.md` for more shapes.
169	
170	## Workflow D — block until tasks reach terminal state
171	
172	```bash
173	# Wait for specific ids
174	skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/wait.py --ids 17,18,19 --timeout-seconds 300
175	
176	# Wait for everything in a group
177	skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/wait.py --group ml
178	
179	# Wait for a label prefix (e.g. all tasks the DAG submitter created)
180	skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/wait.py --label-prefix nightly-
181	```
182	
183	Output is a JSON summary on stdout:
184	
185	```json
186	{"summary": {"total": 4, "success": 3, "failed": 1, "killed": 0, "dependency_failed": 0},
187	 "tasks": [{"id": 17, "status": "Done", "result": "Success", "exit_code": 0,
188	            "label": "nightly-fetch", "group": "ml",
189	            "start": "...", "end": "..."}],
190	 "elapsed_seconds": 42.3}
191	```
192	
193	Exit codes: `0` all succeeded, `5` ≥1 task failed/killed/dependency-failed,
194	`6` timeout. The agent can branch on exit code instead of parsing JSON.
195	
196	## Workflow E — logs, retry, kill
197	
198	One-line `pueue` calls (full list in `references/cli-cheatsheet.md`):
199	
200	```bash
201	pueue log --json --full 17        # full stdout/stderr as JSON
202	pueue restart --in-place 17       # retry in-place (overwrites old log)
203	pueue kill 17 && pueue remove 17  # kill + drop from queue
204	```
205	
206	For ad-hoc filtering, prefer pueue's built-in QUERY DSL over piping
207	through `jq` — it's faster (server-side filter) and shorter:
208	
209	```bash
210	pueue status --json 'status=Failed order_by end desc first 10'
211	pueue status --json 'label %= sweep-'   # substring match
212	```
213	
214	See `references/json-schema.md` for the QUERY grammar + jq fallbacks.
215	
216	## Workflow F — periodic cleanup
217	
218	Pueue's task list grows unbounded. `pueue status --json` walks the whole
219	table, so a queue with thousands of completed tasks slows down everything
220	that touches status. Run `cleanup.sh` weekly:
221	
222	```bash
223	skills/local/pueue-job-queue/scripts/cleanup.sh \
224	  --successful-only --remove-empty-groups --logs-older-than 30
225	# stdout: {"cleaned_tasks":[...], "removed_groups":["dag-abc12345"],
226	#          "deleted_logs":[...], "kept_running":[...], ...}
227	```
228	
229	`--successful-only` keeps failures around for inspection; drop the flag
230	for a full sweep. Pair with the agent's existing weekly maintenance habit
231	(or `/schedule` an agent to run it).
232	
233	## Available scripts
234	
235	- **`scripts/check-daemon.sh`** — Single-shot daemon health + version + log-dir check, with optional auto-start. Outputs JSON to stdout.
236	  - Flags: `--start`, `--json` (default on), `--help`.
237	  - Exit: `0` healthy, `2` pueue not installed, `3` daemon unreachable, `4` client/daemon version mismatch.
238	- **`scripts/submit.sh`** — Submit ONE task, return clean JSON `{task_id, group, label, after, ...}`. Wraps `pueue add --print-task-id` with defensive id parsing. Auto-creates the group if missing.
239	  - Flags: `--label`, `--group`, `--after` (repeatable), `--immediate`, `--stashed`, `--delay`, `--priority`, `--working-dir`, `--escape`, `--dry-run`, `--help`.
240	  - Exit: `0` ok, `1` bad args, `2` pueue not installed, `3` `pueue add` failed, `4` daemon unreachable.
241	- **`scripts/wait.py`** — Block until selected tasks reach terminal status; emit a JSON summary. Selectors: `--ids`, `--label`, `--label-prefix`, `--group`. Quiet by default — emits only one initial line + state-change events on stderr; pass `--verbose` for per-tick output.
242	  - Flags: `--ids`, `--label` (repeatable), `--label-prefix`, `--group`, `--poll-seconds`, `--timeout-seconds`, `--fail-fast`, `--verbose`, `--help`.
243	  - Exit: `0` all succeeded, `1` arg error, `4` daemon unreachable, `5` ≥1 failed/killed/dependency-failed, `6` timeout.
244	- **`scripts/submit-dag.py`** — Declarative DAG submitter. Reads YAML or JSON (file path or `-` for stdin), topo-sorts, validates, submits with wired `--after`, returns `{name → id, topo_order, width_per_group, isolated_group?}`. Computes DAG fan-out width per group; with `--isolated-group [NAME]` creates a fresh dedicated group sized to the width (preferred — leaves user's other groups untouched). With `--auto-parallel` mutates target groups in place. Without either, only warns.
245	  - Flags: `--format`, `--default-group`, `--label-prefix`, `--dry-run`, `--print-graph`, `--auto-parallel`, `--isolated-group [NAME]`, `--help`.
246	  - Exit: `0` all submitted, `1` schema/cycle/unknown-ref/conflicting flags, `2` pueue not installed, `3` mid-run pueue failure (stdout still emits IDs that DID submit, for cleanup).
247	- **`scripts/cleanup.sh`** — Prune pueue task history, empty groups, and old log files. Wraps `pueue clean` + `pueue group remove` for empty non-default groups + optional log-file mtime pruning. Emits a JSON report. Run weekly to keep `pueue status --json` fast.
248	  - Flags: `--successful-only`, `--group GROUP`, `--remove-empty-groups`, `--logs-older-than N`, `--dry-run`, `--help`.
249	  - Exit: `0` ok (or dry-run), `1` bad args, `2` pueue not installed, `3` daemon unreachable.
250	
251	## Bundled assets
252	
253	- `assets/dag.example.yaml` — 5-task fan-out/fan-in (`fetch → featurize → {train_a, train_b} → evaluate`). Pass it to `submit-dag.py` with `--dry-run` first to see the topo order.
254	- `assets/pueue.yml.example` — Config snippet showing `pause_group_on_failure: true`, `default_parallel_tasks`, and a sample `groups:` block. The header comment names the platform-specific destination paths.
255	
256	## Reference files
257	
258	- `references/cli-cheatsheet.md` — Read **when** the task needs `pueue follow`, `pueue log`, `pueue restart`, `pueue kill`, `pueue clean`, `pueue group/parallel`, `pueue pause/start`, `pueue reset`, `pueue edit`, `pueue env`, or any other un-wrapped `pueue` subcommand. Has a one-line "when to use" for each.
259	- `references/json-schema.md` — Read **when** writing custom `jq` queries against `pueue status --json` or `pueue log --json`, or when a script's JSON parsing surprises you. Documents the observed schema on pueue 4.0.2 with concrete examples for each status variant.
260	- `references/dag-patterns.md` — Read **when** the user asks for shapes beyond fan-out/fan-in (mixed sequential+parallel, diamond, etc.) or hits the AND-only / success-only limitation. Has examples and a "when to escalate to a real orchestrator" decision table.
261	- `references/daemon-and-config.md` — Read **when** setting up `pueued` for the first time, configuring per-OS paths, picking config knobs (`pause_group_on_failure`, `default_parallel_tasks`), or wiring up launchd / systemd-user.
262	- `references/remote-daemon.md` — Read **when** the daemon is on another machine: SSH unix-socket forwarding (recommended, needs no server change), direct TCP + TLS, and the working-directory trap that makes cross-platform remote *submission* impractical. Short version: `ssh host 'pueue add ...'` to submit; a forwarded client to read/control.
263	
264	## See also
265	
266	- `long-running-jobs` — pueue is one *implementation* of "let the queue own the
267	  chain" (`--after`) and "block once" (`wait.py`). That skill owns the prior
268	  question: **which** of those an agent should reach for, when a scheduled
269	  check-in is ever justified, and how to record completion durably so a run
270	  survives losing the session. Read it if you are tempted to poll
271	  `pueue status` on a timer.
272	- `slurm-hpc` — the cluster-side equivalent when jobs leave this machine.
273	
274	## Gotchas
275	
276	- **DAG fan-out is gated by `parallel_tasks` per group.** Even when two siblings both depend only on `A` and the DAG allows them to run in parallel, they will *serialize* if their group's `parallel_tasks=1`. Pueue's parallelism primitive is the group, not the dependency graph. `submit-dag.py` warns when DAG width exceeds the group's slots and suggests the exact `pueue parallel N --group G` command; pass `--auto-parallel` to apply it.
277	- **`pueue add -- bash -c 'sleep 60'` does not preserve quoting.** Pueue joins all `<COMMAND>` args and re-shells. The single-quoted `'sleep 60'` is unwrapped by *your* shell before pueue sees it, then pueue re-splits. Quote the **whole** command as one arg: `pueue add 'sleep 60'` or `submit.sh -- 'bash -c "sleep 60 && echo done"'`.
278	- **`--after` is AND-only and success-only.** Failed parent → dependent's `status.Done.result` becomes `"DependencyFailed"` and it never runs. There is no OR, no run-on-failure, no retry-on-failure. If you need that, you need a real orchestrator.
279	- **Pueue does NOT auto-create groups.** `pueue add --group new_name` exits 1 with `"Group new_name doesn't exists. Use one of these: [...]"`. `submit.sh` calls `pueue group add` first if the group is missing.
280	- **`pueue restart` (default) creates a NEW task id.** The old id stays in history with its result. To retry in-place (reusing the id, overwriting the log), pass `--in-place`. Choose deliberately — agent users often want `--in-place` for "retry this".
281	- **`pause_group_on_failure` is config-only, no CLI flag.** Set it in `pueue.yml`; reload with `pueue reset` or restart `pueued`.
282	- **Logs live in platform-specific dirs**, not your CWD. macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/logs/`. Linux: `~/.local/share/pueue/logs/`. Windows: `%APPDATA%\pueue\logs\`. `pueue log --json --full <id>` reads them for you.
283	- **`pueue wait` returns 0 even if the waited-on tasks failed.** It blocks until terminal, period. To know success/failure, query `pueue status --json` afterward (or use `wait.py`, which does this for you and returns a non-zero exit on failures).
284	- **`pueue remove` requires each id as a separate positional arg** (not a space-joined string from a subshell). Use bash arrays: `IDS=($(...)) && pueue remove "${IDS[@]}"`.
285	- **`pueue clean --successful-only` is a flag, not the default.** Plain `pueue clean` removes ALL finished tasks (including failures, which you may want to keep for debugging). Be deliberate.
286	- **`pueue add --print-task-id` writes the bare integer to stdout.** No JSON, no prose. `submit.sh` parses with a regex that tolerates future format changes; if you bypass `submit.sh`, capture with `ID=$(pueue add --print-task-id ... )` directly.
287	- **A terminal result that isn't `Success` is a failure — don't enumerate the bad ones.** `result` is a tagged enum, and `{"FailedToSpawn": "<os error>"}` is dict-shaped, not the bare string older notes implied. Matching a known-bad list let it fall through as success, so `wait.py` returned `0` for a task that never started. It now allowlists `Success` and fails closed on anything else.
288	- **Driving a remote daemon: the working directory is resolved on the CLIENT.** `pueue add` records and canonicalizes the cwd locally, so submitting to a remote daemon fails three different ways — local cwd sent (task ends `FailedToSpawn`), remote-only path rejected outright (`Failed to canonicalize given working directory path`), or a macOS symlink silently rewritten (`/tmp` → `/private/tmp`). Use `ssh host 'pueue add ...'` to submit; a forwarded client is for reading and control. See `references/remote-daemon.md`.
289
```

10	import type { Mutation } from "./transport";
11	
12	export function argvFor(m: Mutation): string[] {
13	  switch (m.op) {
14	    case "add": {
15	      const a = ["add"];
16	      if (m.workingDirectory) a.push("--working-directory", m.workingDirectory);
17	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
18	      if (m.label) a.push("--label", m.label);
19	      if (m.priority !== undefined) a.push("--priority", String(m.priority));
20	      for (const id of m.after ?? []) a.push("--after", String(id));
21	      if (m.delay) a.push("--delay", m.delay);
22	      if (m.stashed) a.push("--stashed");
23	      if (m.immediate) a.push("--immediate");
24	      if (m.escape) a.push("--escape");
25	      a.push("--print-task-id");
26	      // The command goes last, after `--`, as ONE argv element. pueue joins its
27	      // variadic <COMMAND>... with spaces and hands the result to `sh -c`, so
28	      // quoting it here would double-escape it. Never build a shell string.
29	      a.push("--", m.command);
30	      return a;
31	    }
32	    case "start": {
33	      const a = ["start"];
34	      if (m.all) a.push("--all");
35	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
36	      a.push(...(m.ids ?? []).map(String));
37	      return a;
38	    }
39	    case "pause": {
40	      const a = ["pause"];
41	      if (m.all) a.push("--all");
42	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
43	      if (m.wait) a.push("--wait");
44	      a.push(...(m.ids ?? []).map(String));
45	      return a;
46	    }
47	    case "kill": {
48	      const a = ["kill"];
49	      if (m.all) a.push("--all");
50	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
51	      if (m.signal) a.push("--signal", m.signal);
52	      a.push(...(m.ids ?? []).map(String));
53	      return a;
54	    }
55	    case "restart": {
56	      const a = ["restart"];
57	      // Both --in-place and --not-in-place exist because the default comes from
58	      // the user's config. Being explicit means the action does what it says
59	      // regardless of whose machine it runs on.
60	      a.push(m.inPlace ? "--in-place" : "--not-in-place");
61	      if (m.stashed) a.push("--stashed");
62	      if (m.immediate) a.push("--immediate");
63	      a.push(...m.ids.map(String));
64	      return a;
65	    }
66	    case "remove":
67	      return ["remove", ...m.ids.map(String)];
68	    case "stash": {
69	      const a = ["stash"];
70	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
71	      if (m.delay) a.push("--delay", m.delay);
72	      a.push(...(m.ids ?? []).map(String));
73	      return a;
74	    }
75	    case "enqueue": {
76	      const a = ["enqueue"];
77	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
78	      if (m.delay) a.push("--delay", m.delay);
79	      a.push(...(m.ids ?? []).map(String));
80	      return a;
81	    }
82	    case "clean": {
83	      const a = ["clean"];
84	      if (m.successfulOnly) a.push("--successful-only");
85	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
86	      return a;
87	    }
88	    case "switch":
89	      return ["switch", String(m.a), String(m.b)];
90	    case "parallel": {
91	      const a = ["parallel", String(m.count)];
92	      if (m.group) a.push("--group", m.group);
93	      return a;
94	    }
95	    case "group-add": {
96	      const a = ["group", "add", m.name];
97	      if (m.parallel !== undefined) a.push("--parallel", String(m.parallel));
98	      return a;
99	    }
100	    case "group-remove":
101	      return ["group", "remove", m.name];
102	    case "send":
103	      return ["send", String(m.id), m.input];
104	    case "reset": {
105	      const a = ["reset", "--force"];
106	      for (const g of m.groups ?? []) a.push("--groups", g);
107	      return a;
108	    }
109	  }
110	}
111	
112	/** The subcommand path an argv addresses, e.g. ["group","add"]. For flag checking. */
113	export function subcommandOf(argv: string[]): string[] {
114	  return argv[0] === "group" ? argv.slice(0, 2) : argv.slice(0, 1);
115	}
116	
117	/** Long flags an argv uses, in order. For checking against `--help`. */
118	export function longFlagsOf(argv: string[]): string[] {
119	  const out: string[] = [];
120	  for (const a of argv) {
121	    if (a === "--") break;
122	    if (a.startsWith("--")) out.push(a);
123	  }
124	  return out;
125	}

9	import type { Task, TaskResult, TaskStatus } from "./types";
10	
11	export type StatusKind =
12	  | "stashed"
13	  | "queued"
14	  | "running"
15	  | "paused"
16	  | "locked"
17	  | "done"
18	  /** A pueue version newer than we know about. Degrade, never throw. */

21	export type ResultKind =
22	  | "success"
23	  | "failed"
24	  | "failed-to-spawn"
25	  | "killed"

27	  | "dependency-failed"
28	  | "unknown";
29	
30	const STATUS_KINDS: Record<string, StatusKind> = {
31	  Stashed: "stashed",
32	  Queued: "queued",
33	  Running: "running",
34	  Paused: "paused",
35	  Locked: "locked",
36	  Done: "done",
37	};
38	
39	/** The outer variant tag. `Locked` reports as "locked" — see `underlyingKind`. */
40	export function statusKind(s: TaskStatus): StatusKind {
41	  const tag = Object.keys(s)[0];

43	}
44	
45	/**
46	 * `Locked` wraps the status the task will return to once editing finishes, and

48	 */

50	  return "Locked" in s ? unwrapLocked(s.Locked.previous_status) : s;
51	}
52

54	export function underlyingKind(s: TaskStatus): StatusKind {
55	  return statusKind(unwrapLocked(s));
56	}
57	
58	export function isLocked(s: TaskStatus): boolean {

60	}
61	
62	/** The `TaskResult`, or undefined when the task hasn't finished. */
63	export function taskResult(s: TaskStatus): TaskResult | undefined {
64	  const u = unwrapLocked(s);

66	}
67	
68	export function resultKind(r: TaskResult | undefined): ResultKind | undefined {
69	  if (r === undefined) return undefined;
70	  if (typeof r === "string") {
71	    switch (r) {
72	      case "Success":
73	        return "success";
74	      case "Killed":
75	        return "killed";
76	      case "Errored":
77	        return "errored";
78	      case "DependencyFailed":
79	        return "dependency-failed";
80	      default:

82	    }

84	  if ("Failed" in r) return "failed";
85	  if ("FailedToSpawn" in r) return "failed-to-spawn";

153	export function isPueueErrorOutput(output: string | undefined): boolean {

156	
157	/** The task's real output, or undefined when there isn't any. */
158	export function cleanLogOutput(output: string | undefined): string | undefined {
159	  if (!output || isPueueErrorOutput(output)) return undefined;
160	  const trimmed = output.replace(/\s+$/, "");

173	 * fractional digits and truncates to milliseconds.
174	 */
175	export function parseTs(s: string | null | undefined): Date | undefined {
176	  if (!s) return undefined;
177	  const d = new Date(s);
178	  return Number.isNaN(d.getTime()) ? undefined : d;
179	}
180	
181	/**

186	 */
187	export function enqueuedAt(s: TaskStatus): Date | undefined {
188	  const u = unwrapLocked(s);

190	  if ("Queued" in u) return parseTs(u.Queued.enqueued_at);
191	  if ("Running" in u) return parseTs(u.Running.enqueued_at);
192	  if ("Paused" in u) return parseTs(u.Paused.enqueued_at);

200	  if ("Paused" in u) return parseTs(u.Paused.start);
201	  if ("Done" in u) return parseTs(u.Done.start);

211	export function durationMs(t: Task, now = Date.now()): number | undefined {

214	  const end = endedAt(t.status);
215	  return (end ? end.getTime() : now) - start.getTime();
216	}

222	  failed: "failed",
223	  "failed-to-spawn": "failed to spawn",
224	  killed: "killed",
225	  errored: "errored",
226	  "dependency-failed": "dependency failed",

229	
230	/** A short human label: "running", "failed (127)", "killed", "stashed until …". */

247	
248	/**

250	 * which is how search works — the whole state is already in memory, and the

259	    t.original_command,

270	/** Collapse whitespace and ellipsize — commands are frequently multi-line pipelines. */
271	export function oneline(s: string, max = 80): string {
272	  const flat = s.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
273	  return flat.length > max ? `${flat.slice(0, max - 1)}…` : flat;

276	/** The tasks map as a list, ordered by id ascending. */
277	export function taskList(tasks: Record<string, Task>): Task[] {
278	  return Object.values(tasks).sort((a, b) => a.id - b.id);
279	}

1	/**
2	 * The Pueue wire format, 1:1 with `pueue_lib` v4.0.4's serde output.
3	 *
4	 * No I/O lives here. These types are deliberately a literal transcription of
5	 * the Rust structs rather than something ergonomic — the ergonomic view is
6	 * built on top in `normalize.ts`. Keeping the transcription honest is what
7	 * makes the normalizers trustworthy.
8	 *
9	 * v4.0.0 was a hard break: timestamps and results moved *into* the status
10	 * enum. Any v3-era example you find online has flat `start`/`end`/`result`
11	 * fields on Task and will not parse.
12	 */
13	
14	/**
15	 * Externally tagged, and it mixes bare strings with single-field objects —
16	 * `"Success"` but `{"Failed": 127}`. Both shapes must be handled.
17	 */
18	export type TaskResult =
19	  | "Success"
20	  | "Killed"
21	  | "Errored"
22	  | "DependencyFailed"
23	  /** Non-zero exit; the number is the exit code. */
24	  | { Failed: number }
25	  /** Couldn't spawn at all — bad cwd, typo'd binary. The string is the OS error. */
26	  | { FailedToSpawn: string };
27	
28	/**
29	 * Externally tagged and recursive through `Locked`. There is NO flat
30	 * `"status": "Running"` string anywhere in a Task.
31	 *
32	 * Note the one-letter split: `Stashed` carries `enqueue_at` (when it *will* be
33	 * enqueued, nullable), every other variant carries `enqueued_at` (when it
34	 * *was*). Getting this wrong fails silently as `undefined`.
35	 */
36	export type TaskStatus =
37	  | { Stashed: { enqueue_at: string | null } }
38	  | { Queued: { enqueued_at: string } }
39	  | { Running: { enqueued_at: string; start: string } }
40	  | { Paused: { enqueued_at: string; start: string } }
41	  /** Set while `pueue edit` holds the task. Wraps the status it will return to. */
42	  | { Locked: { previous_status: TaskStatus } }
43	  | {
44	      Done: {
45	        enqueued_at: string;
46	        start: string;
47	        end: string;
48	        result: TaskResult;
49	      };
50	    };
51	
52	/** Exactly what `status --json` puts in `tasks["<id>"]`. */
53	export interface RawTask {
54	  id: number;
55	  created_at: string;
56	  original_command: string;
57	  command: string;
58	  path: string;
59	  /**
60	   * A full snapshot of the submitting shell's environment. Upstream cites
61	   * ~2 MB of state for 400 tasks, virtually all of it this field, and it may
62	   * contain secrets. Dropped at the parse boundary — see `Task`.
63	   */
64	  envs: Record<string, string>;
65	  group: string;
66	  dependencies: number[];
67	  priority: number;
68	  label: string | null;
69	  status: TaskStatus;
70	}
71	
72	/**
73	 * The app-facing task. `envs` is dropped in `cli-transport.ts` before anything
74	 * can render it or write it to Raycast's disk-backed cache. Fetch it on demand
75	 * with `taskEnvs(id)` if a view genuinely needs it.
76	 */
77	export type Task = Omit<RawTask, "envs">;
78	
79	export type GroupStatus = "Running" | "Paused" | "Reset";
80	
81	export interface Group {
82	  status: GroupStatus;
83	  /** 0 means unlimited. */
84	  parallel_tasks: number;
85	}
86	
87	/** `status --json` top level. Task ids are the map keys, as strings. */
88	export interface State {
89	  tasks: Record<string, Task>;
90	  groups: Record<string, Group>;
91	}
92	
93	/**
94	 * `group --json` returns the INNER map only — `{"default": {...}}`, NOT
95	 * `{"groups": {...}}`. A different top-level shape from `status --json`;
96	 * feeding one parser to both is the easiest bug in this codebase.
97	 */
98	export type GroupMap = Record<string, Group>;
99	
100	/** `log --json` → `{"<id>": {task, output}}`. Pueue blanks `task.envs` here. */
101	export interface LogEntry {
102	  task: Task;
103	  output: string;
104	}
105	
106	export type LogMap = Record<string, LogEntry>;
107	
108	/**
109	 * A timestamped read. The menu bar keeps data and its age in one cache entry
110	 * so the two can never drift apart.
111	 */
112	export interface Snapshot {
113	  state: State;
114	  fetchedAt: number;
115	}

1	# This-repo conventions
2	
3	Conventions specific to the `daviddwlee84/agent-skills` repository. Skills
4	authored elsewhere may follow different rules; this file is the source of
5	truth for **this** repo.
6	
7	## Layout
8	
9	```
10	skills/
11	├── local/             # skills authored in this repo (committed in full)
12	│   └── <skill-name>/
13	│       ├── SKILL.md
14	│       ├── references/
15	│       ├── scripts/
16	│       └── assets/
17	└── vendor/            # skills cherry-picked from upstream repos
18	    └── <skill-name>/
19	        └── ...        # synced via scripts/sync-vendor.sh
20	```
21	
22	- **New skills authored here go in `skills/local/`.** Always.
23	- **Don't manually edit anything in `skills/vendor/`** — it gets overwritten by
24	  the next `make sync`. Upstream changes go through `vendor.yaml` + `make sync`.
25	- **`.agents/skills/` and `.claude/skills/` at the repo root are active
26	  discovery-symlink farms**, not legacy. Each entry under them is a relative
27	  symlink (`../../skills/local/<name>` or `../../skills/vendor/<name>`) so
28	  that Cursor / Codex / Warp / OpenCode (`.agents/skills/`) and Claude Code
29	  (`.claude/skills/`) can dogfood the skills authored in this repo. The
30	  `new-skill.sh` scaffolder creates these symlinks automatically in **LOCAL
31	  mode**; never add new *canonical* skill content directly under them here.
32	
33	## `new-skill.sh` placement scopes
34	
35	`scripts/new-skill.sh` supports three placement scopes that mirror the
36	behavior of `npx skills add` (`vercel-labs/skills`). Auto-detection
37	precedence (when no flag given):
38	
39	1. **LOCAL** — publishing-repo anchor (`vendor.yaml`, `skills/local/`, or
40	   `skills/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`) found walking up. This is the
41	   default *inside this very repo*. Canonical content lives in
42	   `<repo>/skills/local/<name>/` (or `skills/vendor/<name>/` with
43	   `--vendor`); the script adds the `.agents/skills/` + `.claude/skills/`
44	   discovery symlinks for you.
45	2. **PROJECT** — a git root found walking up. Canonical content goes to
46	   `<repo>/.agents/skills/<name>/` (universal agents like Cursor / Codex /
47	   OpenCode / Warp / Gemini-CLI / Copilot read this directly); a relative
48	   symlink `<repo>/.claude/skills/<name> -> ../../.agents/skills/<name>` is
49	   added for Claude Code, plus links for any other non-universal agent dir
50	   (e.g. `.windsurf/`, `.continue/`) that already exists at the repo root.
51	3. **GLOBAL** — neither anchor found, or `--global` forced. Same shape as
52	   PROJECT but rooted at `$HOME`: canonical at `~/.agents/skills/<name>/`,
53	   plus `~/.claude/skills/<name>` and any other already-present
54	   `~/.<agent>/skills/` link.
55	
56	The fan-out rule is "claude-code always, others only if their config root
57	already exists at the base dir" — this mirrors `npx skills add`'s
58	"don't create `.windsurf/` unless the project already uses Windsurf"
59	behavior. The script never creates a new top-level agent home dir.
60	
61	Symlinks are always *relative* with a fixed `../../` prefix because both
62	the link's parent (`.../skills/`) and the canonical dir
63	(`.../.agents/skills/` or `.../skills/local/`) are exactly two levels under
64	the base dir. See [`pitfalls/symlink-target-relative-to-symlink-not-cwd.md`](../../../../pitfalls/symlink-target-relative-to-symlink-not-cwd.md)
65	for the historical bug this convention prevents.
66	
67	## Skill discovery
68	
69	The `skills` CLI looks for `SKILL.md` files like this:
70	
71	1. **First pass:** one level deep — `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
72	2. **Fallback:** recursive up to **5 levels** if first pass found nothing
73	   useful.
74	
75	That's why `skills/local/<name>/SKILL.md` and `skills/vendor/<name>/SKILL.md`
76	both work — they're 2 levels deep, well within the recursive fallback. **Don't
77	nest a skill more than 5 levels deep** or it becomes invisible.
78	
79	## Scripts naming and mirroring
80	
81	Some scripts are bundled into a skill **and** mirrored to `scripts/` at repo
82	root. The pattern:
83	
84	| Canonical location | Mirror |
85	|---|---|
86	| `skills/local/project-knowledge-harness/scripts/add-todo.sh` | `scripts/add-todo.sh` |
87	| `skills/local/project-knowledge-harness/scripts/sweep-inbox.sh` | `scripts/sweep-inbox.sh` |
88	| `skills/local/project-knowledge-harness/scripts/promote-todo.sh` | `scripts/promote-todo.sh` |
89	| `skills/local/project-knowledge-harness/scripts/todo-kanban.sh` | `scripts/todo-kanban.sh` |
90	
91	Reason: the canonical copy travels with the skill (downstream consumers get it
92	via `init.sh`). The root-level mirror is for *this* repo's own use so `make`
93	targets and CI don't have to know the skill's path.
94	
95	**Mirrors must stay byte-identical.** If you edit one, run the equivalent
96	`cp` to update the other and verify with `diff`. There is currently no
97	automated check for this — be careful.
98	
99	## Documentation
100	
101	- `README.md` — short repo entrypoint with install snippet.
102	- `docs/` — built into a MkDocs Material site at
103	  `https://daviddwlee84.github.io/agent-skills/`.
104	- `docs/skills/<skill-name>.md` — user-facing docs for each local skill. Link
105	  back to the canonical SKILL.md on GitHub via absolute URL (see linking rules
106	  in `docs/reference/docs-stack-recipe.md`).
107	
108	When you add a new local skill, also add:
109	
110	1. A row to `docs/skills/index.md`.
111	2. A `docs/skills/<skill-name>.md` page (can be short; cross-link to SKILL.md).
112	3. A nav entry in `mkdocs.yml`.
113	4. A row to the README's "What's in here" table.
114	
115	## Project memory
116	
117	This repo uses the `project-knowledge-harness` skill on itself. That means:
118	
119	- `TODO.md` is structured (P1/P2/P3/P?/Done sections, validated by
120	  `scripts/todo-kanban.sh --validate-only`).
121	- `backlog/inbox.md` is the loose-capture inbox.
122	- `backlog/<slug>.md` holds research notes for non-trivial items.
123	- `pitfalls/<slug>.md` holds debugging traps with symptom-first titles.
124	
125	When authoring a skill, if you discover a non-obvious trap, write it to
126	`pitfalls/`. Don't bury it in commit messages or chat history.
127	
128	## AGENTS.md ↔ CLAUDE.md
129	
130	`AGENTS.md` is a **symlink** to `CLAUDE.md`. Edit either one. Don't replace
131	the symlink with a real file or they'll drift.
132	
133	## Bash compatibility
134	
135	All bundled scripts must be **bash 3.2 compatible** (stock macOS). See
136	`script-design.md` § "Bash 3.2 compatibility" for the safe subset and
137	escape hatches.
138	
139	## When this repo's conventions conflict with agentskills.io
140	
141	The agentskills.io best practices are upstream / generic; this file is local /
142	specific. When they conflict, this file wins **for skills authored in this
143	repo**. Notable specifics:
144	
145	- We default to bundling helper scripts in `scripts/` rather than relying on
146	  ad-hoc `uvx` invocations, because we want the helpers to compose with the
147	  repo's `Makefile` and CI.
148	- We use Bash for orchestration scripts (TODO management, vendor sync) so they
149	  run without a Python environment. PEP 723 Python is fine for analytical or
150	  parsing-heavy helpers.
151	- Skill descriptions in this repo lean **even pushier** than the agentskills.io
152	  guidance because we're optimizing for the OpenCode/Claude Code default
153	  triggering behavior, which under-triggers more aggressively than Claude.ai.
154
```

```text
1	# Authoring patterns
2	
3	Condensed from <https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices>. Read this
4	before writing or editing a SKILL.md body.
5	
6	## Table of contents
7	
8	1. [Spending context wisely](#spending-context-wisely)
9	2. [Cross-agent frontmatter compatibility](#cross-agent-frontmatter-compatibility)
10	3. [Calibrating control](#calibrating-control)
11	4. [Gotchas sections](#gotchas-sections)
12	5. [Output templates](#output-templates)
13	6. [Checklists for multi-step workflows](#checklists-for-multi-step-workflows)
14	7. [Validation loops](#validation-loops)
15	8. [Plan-validate-execute](#plan-validate-execute)
16	9. [Bundling reusable scripts](#bundling-reusable-scripts)
17	10. [Quick checklist before commit](#quick-checklist-before-commit)
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Spending context wisely
22	
23	Every token in `SKILL.md` competes with the conversation history, the system
24	prompt, and every other active skill. Spend tokens on what the agent **wouldn't
25	know without you**:
26	
27	- Project-specific conventions (table names, repo layout, internal jargon)
28	- Domain-specific procedures with non-obvious steps
29	- Edge cases the agent will misjudge by default
30	- Specific tools/APIs to prefer (with the *why*, briefly)
31	
32	Don't spend tokens on:
33	
34	- Explaining what well-known things are (PDF, HTTP, REST, JSON)
35	- Generic "best practices" the agent already applies (handle errors, write tests)
36	- Comprehensive option enumerations — give a default and one escape hatch
37	
38	**Test:** for each paragraph, ask "would the agent get this wrong without it?"
39	If no, cut it.
40	
41	### Progressive disclosure
42	
43	Three loading levels:
44	
45	| Level | Loaded | Budget |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| Frontmatter (`name`, `description`) | always | 120-500 chars preferred, 1024 max |
48	| `SKILL.md` body | when skill triggers | <500 lines, <5000 tokens |
49	| `references/*.md`, `assets/*`, `scripts/*` | on demand | unlimited |
50	
51	If `SKILL.md` is creeping past 500 lines, move sections to `references/<topic>.md`
52	and reference them with **load conditions** ("Read X if Y happens"), not just
53	"see X for details". Conditions let the agent load on demand; bare pointers tend
54	to either get ignored or get pre-loaded out of caution.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## Cross-agent frontmatter compatibility
59	
60	Use this as the portable baseline for coding agents that consume Agent Skills:
61	
62	- `name`: required, lowercase letters/digits/hyphens only, no leading/trailing
63	  hyphen, no `--`, <=64 characters.
64	- `description`: required, non-empty string, <=1024 characters. Include both
65	  what the skill does and concrete trigger contexts. Keep the first 60
66	  characters meaningful because `npx skills` truncates picker hints there.
67	- **Quoting**: a YAML plain (unquoted) scalar may not contain `": "`, and ` #`
68	  starts a comment. Long English descriptions hit both constantly
69	  (`"…debug a FastAPI app: choosing def vs async def"`). Wrap such values in
70	  single quotes — the whole skill is otherwise skipped at install time with
71	  "Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings", or installs with a
72	  silently truncated description. `scripts/lint-frontmatter.sh` gates this.
73	- Keep `name` and `description` as the only required frontmatter fields for
74	  portability. Agent-specific fields are allowed when needed, but isolate them
75	  intentionally: Cursor uses `disable-model-invocation`, Codex can read
76	  `agents/openai.yaml`, and some vendored skills carry upstream-only metadata.
77	
78	Description budget tiers:
79	
80	| Tier | Length | Meaning |
81	|---|---:|---|
82	| Green | 120-500 chars | Preferred for local skills: enough trigger surface without context bloat |
83	| Yellow | 501-900 chars | Valid, but context-heavy; move details to `SKILL.md` body |
84	| Orange | 901-1024 chars | Valid, but close to hard loader limits |
85	| Red | >1024 chars | Invalid for Codex/Cursor/spec-aligned validators |
86	
87	Agent notes:
88	
89	- **Codex** skips invalid `SKILL.md` files; OpenAI's validator enforces the
90	  64-char name and 1024-char description limits.
91	- **Cursor** managed `create-skill` guidance matches the same 64/1024 limits
92	  and supports `disable-model-invocation` for explicit-only skills.
93	- **Claude Code** uses descriptions for discovery and tolerates additional
94	  frontmatter in practice, but long descriptions still consume always-on
95	  context and are poor picker hints.
96	- **OpenCode** follows the Agent Skills convention and uses descriptions for
97	  invocation; stay within the portable baseline unless a target agent's docs
98	  say otherwise.
99	- **Claude.ai upload** may impose stricter UI limits. Treat that as a separate
100	  packaging target, not the default coding-agent baseline for this repo.
101	
102	---
103	
104	## Calibrating control
105	
106	Match instruction specificity to **task fragility**, not to "we should be thorough".
107	
108	### Be prescriptive when:
109	
110	- The operation is destructive or has side effects
111	- A specific sequence of steps must hold (migration, release, deploy)
112	- An external system requires exact format (API contract, parser input)
113	
114	```markdown
115	## Database migration
116	
117	Run exactly this sequence:
118	
119	    python scripts/migrate.py --verify --backup
120	
121	Do not modify the command or add flags. The `--verify` step seeds an
122	integrity check that later phases depend on.
123	```
124	
125	The trailing sentence is the trick — even when prescriptive, **explain why**.
126	Agents that understand the reason follow it more reliably than agents that just
127	see "DO NOT" in caps.
128	
129	### Give the agent freedom when:
130	
131	- Multiple valid approaches exist
132	- The output is judgment-driven (code review, refactor proposal)
133	- You'd be hand-coding policy if you wrote it all out
134	
135	```markdown
136	## Code review process
137	
138	1. Check database queries for SQL injection (use parameterized queries)
139	2. Verify auth checks on every endpoint
140	3. Look for race conditions in concurrent code paths
141	4. Confirm error messages don't leak internals
142	```
143	
144	Notice: *what to look for*, not *how to look for it*. The agent picks the
145	approach.
146	
147	### Defaults, not menus
148	
149	When several tools could work, pick one default and mention alternatives as
150	escape hatches.
151	
152	```markdown
153	Use pdfplumber for text extraction.
154	
155	For scanned PDFs requiring OCR, fall back to pdf2image with pytesseract.
156	```
157	
158	…not:
159	
160	```markdown
161	You can use pypdf, pdfplumber, PyMuPDF, or pdf2image depending on...
162	```
163	
164	### Procedures over declarations
165	
166	Teach the agent *how* to approach the class of problem, not *what* to produce
167	for one instance.
168	
169	```markdown
170	Bad — only useful for this exact query:
171	  Join `orders` to `customers` on `customer_id`, filter region='EMEA',
172	  sum `amount`.
173	
174	Good — works for any query:
175	  1. Read schema from `references/schema.yaml` to find relevant tables.
176	  2. Join via the `_id` foreign key convention.
177	  3. Apply user-requested filters as WHERE clauses.
178	  4. Aggregate numeric columns and format as a markdown table.
179	```
180	
181	Specifics still belong in the skill (output format templates, "never output
182	PII", tool-specific quirks) — but the *approach* should generalize.
183	
184	---
185	
186	## Gotchas sections
187	
188	Often the single highest-value section in a skill. **Concrete corrections to
189	mistakes the agent will make without being told.** Not generic advice.
190	
191	```markdown
192	## Gotchas
193	
194	- The `users` table uses soft deletes. Queries must include
195	  `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` or results will include deactivated accounts.
196	- The user ID is `user_id` in the database, `uid` in the auth service, and
197	  `accountId` in the billing API. All three refer to the same value.
198	- The `/health` endpoint returns 200 if the web server is up, even if the
199	  database is down. Use `/ready` to check full service health.
200	```
201	
202	Keep gotchas in `SKILL.md`, not in a separate reference. The whole point is
203	that the agent reads them **before** hitting the situation — by the time it
204	realizes it should load `references/gotchas.md`, the bug has happened.
205	
206	**Iteration tip:** every time you correct the agent during a real run, add the
207	correction here. Most skills' gotchas sections grow over weeks, not get written
208	all at once.
209	
210	---
211	
212	## Output templates
213	
214	Agents pattern-match against concrete structures more reliably than they
215	follow prose descriptions. When the output has a fixed shape, paste the shape:
216	
217	````markdown
218	## Report structure
219	
220	Use this template, adapting sections as needed:
221	
222	```markdown
223	# [Analysis Title]
224	
225	## Executive summary
226	[One paragraph]
227	
228	## Key findings
229	- Finding 1 with supporting data
230	- Finding 2 with supporting data
231	
232	## Recommendations
233	1. Specific actionable recommendation
234	2. Specific actionable recommendation
235	```
236	````
237	
238	Long templates or templates that only apply in some cases should live in
239	`assets/<name>.template` and be loaded on demand from `SKILL.md`.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Checklists for multi-step workflows
244	
245	Make dependencies and validation gates visible:
246	
247	```markdown
248	## Form processing workflow
249	
250	Progress:
251	- [ ] 1. Analyze the form  → `scripts/analyze_form.py`
252	- [ ] 2. Create field mapping  → edit `fields.json`
253	- [ ] 3. Validate mapping  → `scripts/validate_fields.py`
254	- [ ] 4. Fill the form  → `scripts/fill_form.py`
255	- [ ] 5. Verify output  → `scripts/verify_output.py`
256	```
257	
258	The agent treats the checkboxes as state and won't skip to step 4 without
259	ticking 1-3. Dependency arrows make the wiring explicit.
260	
261	---
262	
263	## Validation loops
264	
265	For tasks where output quality is testable, instruct the agent to validate
266	and re-try, not "do your best and stop":
267	
268	```markdown
269	## Editing workflow
270	
271	1. Make your edits.
272	2. Run validation: `python scripts/validate.py output/`
273	3. If validation fails:
274	   - Read the error message.
275	   - Fix the issues.
276	   - Run validation again.
277	4. Only proceed when validation passes.
278	```
279	
280	The validator can be a script, a reference checklist, or a self-check prompt.
281	The pattern is identical: **do → validate → fix → re-validate → proceed**.
282	
283	---
284	
285	## Plan-validate-execute
286	
287	For batch or destructive operations, force the agent through an intermediate
288	**plan artifact** that gets validated before any side effects happen:
289	
290	```markdown
291	## PDF form filling
292	
293	1. Extract form fields:
294	   `python scripts/analyze_form.py input.pdf`  → `form_fields.json`
295	2. Create `field_values.json` mapping each field name to its intended value.
296	3. Validate:
297	   `python scripts/validate_fields.py form_fields.json field_values.json`
298	   (checks every field exists, types match, required fields present)
299	4. If validation fails, revise `field_values.json` and re-validate.
300	5. Fill the form:
301	   `python scripts/fill_form.py input.pdf field_values.json output.pdf`
302	```
303	
304	The magic is step 3. A validator that catches "field 'signature_date' not
305	found — available: customer_name, order_total, signature_date_signed" lets the
306	agent self-correct **before** the destructive step 5.
307	
308	This pattern eliminates an entire class of "oops, ran the wrong thing on prod"
309	failures. Use it any time the actual operation is hard to undo.
310	
311	---
312	
313	## Bundling reusable scripts
314	
315	When you iterate on a skill (with `skill-creator`), watch the agent transcripts
316	across test runs. If the agent independently reinvents the same logic each run
317	— building the same chart, parsing the same format, validating the same way —
318	that's a signal to write the script once and bundle it in `scripts/`.
319	
320	Heuristic: if you see the same ~20-line helper appearing in 2+ runs, bundle it.
321	
322	See `references/script-design.md` for **how** to design bundled scripts so an
323	agent can call them reliably.
324	
325	---
326	
327	## Quick checklist before commit
328	
329	Before considering a SKILL.md "done":
330	
331	- [ ] Description includes specific trigger contexts ("use when X, Y, Z"),
332	      not just a one-line summary
333	- [ ] Description is "pushy" but within budget: 120-500 chars preferred,
334	      <=1024 chars required
335	- [ ] First 60 description chars are useful in picker UIs
336	- [ ] Name is hyphen-case and <=64 chars
337	- [ ] SKILL.md is under 500 lines (move overflow into `references/`)
338	- [ ] Every `references/*.md` is mentioned with a load condition, not just
339	      listed at the bottom
340	- [ ] Has a `## Gotchas` section (or an honest reason it's empty)
341	- [ ] Output format, if structured, is shown as a literal template
342	- [ ] Multi-step procedures use checklists with dependencies marked
343	- [ ] Destructive operations go through plan-validate-execute or have
344	      `--dry-run` support
345	- [ ] Bundled scripts are listed under `## Available scripts` with their flags
346	- [ ] No "MUST" / "ALWAYS" / "NEVER" in caps without an accompanying *why*
347

74	  }, RECONCILE_DELAY_MS);

77	export interface ActOptions {

79	  verb: string;
80	  /** Past tense, e.g. "Killed task 4". */
81	  done: string;
82	  confirm?: {

84	    message?: string;

86	    actionTitle?: string;
87	    destructive?: boolean;

89	    rememberChoice?: boolean;

91	  /** Which daemon to act on. Omitted means the default connection. */
92	  connection?: Connection;
93	}

96	 * Run a mutation with an optimistic paint and a delayed reconcile.
97	 *
98	 * Generic over what the calling hook holds, because the two list views cache
99	 * different shapes: Tasks caches a whole `State`, Groups caches a `GroupMap`.
100	 * Each supplies the pure updater for its own shape.
101	 *
102	 * Returns true when the mutation ran (i.e. wasn't cancelled at the confirmation).
103	 */
104	export async function act<T>(
105	  mutation: Mutation,
106	  state: { mutate: MutatePromise<T | undefined>; revalidate: () => void },
107	  options: ActOptions,
108	  optimistic: (data: T | undefined, m: Mutation) => T | undefined,
109	): Promise<boolean> {
110	  const prefs = getPreferenceValues<Preferences>();
111	
112	  if (options.confirm && prefs.confirmDestructive) {
113	    const ok = await confirmAlert({
114	      title: options.confirm.title,
115	      message: options.confirm.message,
116	      rememberUserChoice: options.confirm.rememberChoice,
117	      primaryAction: {
118	        title: options.confirm.actionTitle ?? options.verb,
119	        style: options.confirm.destructive
120	          ? Alert.ActionStyle.Destructive
121	          : Alert.ActionStyle.Default,
122	      },
123	    });
124	    if (!ok) return false;
125	  }
126	
127	  const toast = await showToast({
128	    style: Toast.Style.Animated,
129	    title: options.verb,
130	  });
131	
132	  try {
133	    await state.mutate(
134	      runMutation(mutation, { connection: options.connection }),
135	      {
136	        optimisticUpdate: (data) => optimistic(data, mutation),
137	        rollbackOnError: true,
138	        // The load-bearing line. See the module comment.
139	        shouldRevalidateAfter: false,
140	      },

143	    toast.style = Toast.Style.Success;
144	    toast.title = options.done;

147	    setTimeout(() => state.revalidate(), RECONCILE_SETTLE_MS);

150	  } catch (error) {

152	    // Its prose is better than anything we'd write, so show it.
153	    await showFailureToast(error, {
154	      title: options.verb,
155	      message:
156	        error instanceof PueueError ? firstLine(error.detail) : undefined,
157	    });
158	    return false;
159	  }
160	}
161

1	/**
2	 * What the queue will look like once a mutation lands.
3	 *
4	 * This exists because of one pueue behaviour: the daemon acknowledges a request
5	 * *before* its own update loop has applied it, so the very next
6	 * `pueue status --json` can still report the old state. `useCachedPromise`'s
7	 * `mutate` revalidates immediately by default, which would read that stale
8	 * state and visually undo the optimistic update — the row would flip, flip
9	 * back, and then flip forward again a minute later.
10	 *
11	 * So the UI paints this prediction, suppresses the automatic revalidate, and
12	 * reconciles on a short delay instead.
13	 *
14	 * Pure and total: no I/O, no React, and never throws. A mutation whose outcome
15	 * cannot be predicted (a new task id, a queue reordering) returns the state
16	 * unchanged rather than guessing — a wrong prediction is worse than none.
17	 */
18	
19	// Imported from the leaf modules rather than the `pueue` barrel on purpose:
20	// the barrel pulls in the transport and therefore @raycast/api, and this module
21	// must stay runnable outside Raycast so `just verify` can assert it.
22	import {
23	  enqueuedAt,
24	  isDone,
25	  isSuccess,
26	  startedAt,
27	  underlyingKind,
28	} from "./pueue/normalize";
29	import type { Mutation } from "./pueue/transport";
30	import type { Group, GroupMap, State, Task, TaskResult } from "./pueue/types";
31	
32	const iso = (d: Date | undefined, fallback: string): string =>
33	  (d ?? new Date(fallback)).toISOString();
34	
35	function clone(state: State): State {
36	  return { tasks: { ...state.tasks }, groups: { ...state.groups } };
37	}
38	
39	/**
40	 * Which tasks a mutation touches.
41	 *
42	 * pueue accepts explicit ids, a whole group, or everything; `--group` and
43	 * `--all` are resolved against the states the command actually acts on, so
44	 * "pause the group" doesn't optimistically pause tasks that already finished.
45	 */
46	function targets(
47	  state: State,
48	  m: { ids?: number[]; group?: string; all?: boolean },
49	): Set<number> {
50	  if (m.ids && m.ids.length > 0) return new Set(m.ids);
51	  const all = Object.values(state.tasks);
52	  const scoped = m.all
53	    ? all
54	    : all.filter((t) => t.group === (m.group ?? "default"));
55	  return new Set(scoped.map((t) => t.id));
56	}
57	
58	function mapTasks(
59	  state: State,
60	  ids: Set<number>,
61	  fn: (t: Task) => Task | undefined,
62	): State {
63	  const next = clone(state);
64	  for (const [key, task] of Object.entries(state.tasks)) {
65	    if (!ids.has(task.id)) continue;
66	    const updated = fn(task);
67	    if (updated === undefined) delete next.tasks[key];
68	    else next.tasks[key] = updated;
69	  }
70	  return next;
71	}
72	
73	function setGroupStatus(
74	  state: State,
75	  name: string | undefined,
76	  all: boolean | undefined,
77	  status: Group["status"],
78	): State {
79	  const next = clone(state);
80	  for (const [key, group] of Object.entries(state.groups)) {
81	    if (all || key === (name ?? "default"))
82	      next.groups[key] = { ...group, status };
83	  }
84	  return next;
85	}
86	
87	/** Finish a task now, with the given result. Preserves its existing timestamps. */
88	function finish(task: Task, result: TaskResult): Task {
89	  const now = new Date().toISOString();
90	  return {
91	    ...task,
92	    status: {
93	      Done: {
94	        enqueued_at: iso(enqueuedAt(task.status), now),
95	        start: iso(startedAt(task.status), now),
96	        end: now,
97	        result,
98	      },
99	    },
100	  };
101	}
102	
103	export function applyMutation(state: State | undefined, m: Mutation): State {

144	
145	    case "pause": {

153	                  start: iso(startedAt(t.status), now),
154	                },
155	              },
156	            }
157	          : t,
158	      );
159	      return m.ids && m.ids.length > 0

174	    case "enqueue":

181	    case "remove":

184	    case "clean": {

250	/**

254	 * top-level shape from `status --json`. Only the mutations that change a group

256	 * alone.

258	export function applyGroupMutation(
259	  groups: GroupMap | undefined,
260	  m: Mutation,
261	): GroupMap {
262	  if (!groups) return {};
263	  const next: GroupMap = { ...groups };
264	
265	  const setStatus = (status: Group["status"]) => {
266	    for (const [name, group] of Object.entries(groups)) {
267	      if (m.op === "kill" || m.op === "pause" || m.op === "start") {

269	          next[name] = { ...group, status };

271	      }
272	    }
273	  };
274	
275	  switch (m.op) {
276	    case "pause":
277	      // Only a group-wide pause changes the group's own status; pausing one
278	      // task leaves the group running.
279	      if (m.group || m.all) setStatus("Paused");
280	      return next;
281	
282	    case "start":
283	      if (m.group || m.all) setStatus("Running");
284	      return next;
285	
286	    case "kill":
287	      // Verified in `pueue kill --help`: killing a group also pauses it.
288	      if (m.group || m.all) setStatus("Paused");
289	      return next;
290	
291	    case "parallel": {
292	      const name = m.group ?? "default";
293	      if (next[name]) next[name] = { ...next[name], parallel_tasks: m.count };
294	      return next;
295	    }
296	
297	    case "group-add":
298	      next[m.name] = { status: "Running", parallel_tasks: m.parallel ?? 1 };

301	    case "group-remove":

264	          url: PUEUE_DOCS,
265	        },
266	      ],
267	      structural: false,
268	    };
269	  }
270	
271	  return {
272	    icon: Icon.Warning,
273	    title: firstLine(detail) || "Pueue command failed",
274	    shortTitle: "Pueue error",
275	    description: "Something went wrong talking to pueue.",
276	    markdown: ["# Pueue command failed", "", fence(detail)].join("\n"),
277	    actions: [
278	      { id: "copy", title: "Copy Error", icon: Icon.Clipboard, copy: detail },
279	      {
280	        id: "prefs",
281	        title: "Open Extension Preferences",
282	        icon: Icon.Gear,
283	        run: openExtensionPreferences,
284	      },
285	    ],
286	    structural: false,
287	  };
288	}
289	
290	function renderActions(d: ErrorDescriptor, onRetry?: () => void) {
291	  return (
292	    <ActionPanel>
293	      {d.actions.map((a) =>
294	        a.copy !== undefined ? (
295	          <Action.CopyToClipboard
296	            key={a.id}
297	            title={a.title}
298	            icon={a.icon}
299	            content={a.copy}
300	          />
301	        ) : a.url !== undefined ? (
302	          <Action.OpenInBrowser
303	            key={a.id}
304	            title={a.title}
305	            icon={a.icon}
306	            url={a.url}
307	          />
308	        ) : (
309	          <Action
310	            key={a.id}
311	            title={a.title}
312	            icon={a.icon}
313	            onAction={() => a.run?.()}
314	          />
315	        ),
316	      )}
317	      {onRetry ? (
318	        <Action
319	          title="Reload"
320	          icon={Icon.ArrowClockwise}
321	          shortcut={Keyboard.Shortcut.Common.Refresh}
322	          onAction={onRetry}
323	        />
324	      ) : null}
325	    </ActionPanel>
326	  );
327	}
328	
329	/**
330	 * Must be rendered *inside* a `<List>` — `List.EmptyView` is not standalone.
331	 */
332	export function ErrorEmptyView({
333	  error,
334	  onRetry,
335	  connection,
336	}: {
337	  error: unknown;
338	  onRetry?: () => void;
339	  connection?: { remote: boolean; name: string };
340	}) {
341	  const d = describeError(error, connection);
342	  return (
343	    <List.EmptyView
344	      icon={d.icon}
345	      title={d.title}
346	      description={d.description}
347	      actions={renderActions(d, onRetry)}
348	    />
349	  );
350	}
351	
352	/**
353	 * A row that says the list underneath it can't be trusted.
354	 *
355	 * `useCachedPromise` keeps serving its last successful read when a fetch fails,
356	 * which is the right default — but with the daemon stopped it means a dead
357	 * queue renders as a live one, and Raycast's failure toast is a single line at
358	 * the bottom that scrolls away. A task list that is quietly six hours old is
359	 * worse than no task list, so structural failures get a row of their own,
360	 * carrying the same recovery actions as the full-screen view.
361	 */
362	export function StaleBannerItem({
363	  error,
364	  onRetry,
365	  connection,
366	}: {
367	  error: unknown;
368	  onRetry?: () => void;
369	  connection?: { remote: boolean; name: string };
370	}) {
371	  const d = describeError(error, connection);
372	  return (
373	    <List.Item
374	      icon={{ source: Icon.Warning, tintColor: Color.Red }}
375	      title={d.shortTitle}
376	      accessories={[{ text: "cached" }]}
377	      actions={renderActions(d, onRetry)}
378	    />
379	  );
380	}
381	
382	export function ErrorDetail({
383	  error,
384	  onRetry,
385	  connection,
386	}: {
387	  error: unknown;
388	  onRetry?: () => void;
389	  connection?: { remote: boolean; name: string };
390	}) {
391	  const d = describeError(error, connection);
392	  return <Detail markdown={d.markdown} actions={renderActions(d, onRetry)} />;
393	}
394
